fl.offset.zero: Type an offset distance other than 0.
fl.offset.repeat: The feature line has two vertices in the same place: remove one first.
fl.offset.sharp: A corner turns back too sharply to offset it.
fl.offset.fold: At that distance the offset folds over itself at a bend: use a smaller distance.

sw.head: Swept path
sw.f.name: Name
sw.mode.forward: Forward: the front axle follows the line
sw.mode.reverse: Reversing: the last axle follows the line
sw.mode.note: Draw the line in the direction of travel. Reversing, CivilCraft works out the steering the tractor needs and checks it against the lock.
sw.f.bad: Give every size a number: widths and wheelbases above 0, the lock under 89°.
sw.placeholders: The vehicles to start from are placeholders, not a standard: set the sizes from your own design vehicle.
sw.done: {name}: driven along the line within the steering lock and the articulation limits.
sw.done.problems: {name}: {n} problem(s) along the line; see Properties.
sw.noline: The line this swept path follows is gone or has errors.
sw.ok: Within the steering lock and the articulation limits all along.
sw.prob.steer: At {s} {u} the steering needs {v}°, past the lock of {max}°.
sw.prob.articulation: At {s} {u} trailer {n} turns {v}° against the unit ahead, past its limit of {max}° (it jackknifes).
sw.prob.hitch: Trailer {n}'s hitch is ahead of the axle: reversing, it was taken as on the axle.
sw.prob.short: The line is too short to drive.

fl.tool.hint: Feature line: click its vertices (a survey point gives its elevation, elsewhere the ground's). C turns arcs on: after a vertex, click a point on the curve, then where it ends. Click the first vertex again to close it; Enter finishes.
fl.click.ground: Vertex {n}: its elevation comes from the ground. Enter finishes.
fl.need2: A feature line needs at least two vertices.
fl.need3: A closed feature line needs at least three vertices.
fl.name: Feature line {n}
fl.drawn: {name}: {n} vertices at the ground's elevations. It is a breakline of the existing ground; set its grades and use in Properties.

fl.drawn.guessed.one: 1 vertex was off the surface and took the previous vertex's elevation.
fl.drawn.guessed.other: {n} vertices were off the surface and took the previous vertex's elevation.

fl.props.head: Feature line
fl.props.name: Name
fl.use.note.eg: The existing ground runs through this line at its elevations, like a breakline.
fl.use.note.design: The proposed surface inside this closed line is graded to its edge (a sloped pad). Turn on daylight to run cut and fill slopes out to the ground.
fl.use.note.design.open: Only a closed feature line can be graded into the design: close it, or use it as a breakline of the existing ground.
fl.use.note.off: The line is drawn on the plan and exported, but the surfaces do not use it.
fl.props.closed: Closed (the last vertex joins the first)
fl.props.daylight: Daylight to the ground with cut and fill slopes
fl.props.grade.of: Grade from vertex {n} to the next, in percent
fl.props.grade.note: A grade sets the elevation at the far end of its segment; the vertices after it stay where they are.
fl.props.radius.note: Arc: a radius and L or R (the way it turns, as you walk the line) makes the segment from that vertex an arc, e.g. 50 L; empty makes it straight. Its ends keep their elevations and its grade runs evenly along the arc.
fl.arc.short: Segment {n} is too long for that radius: it needs at least {min}.
fl.arc.on: Arcs on: after a vertex, click a point on the curve, then where it ends. C turns them off.
fl.arc.off: Arcs off: each click is the next vertex.
fl.arc.mid: Point on the curve set: now click where the arc ends.
fl.offset.note: A positive distance offsets to the right of the line's direction, negative to the left. The copy is a new feature line.
fl.offset.numbers: Type numbers for the distance and the height or slope.
fl.offset.name: {name} offset {d}
fl.surface.none: No vertex of this line is on the existing ground.
fl.surface.done: Elevations taken from the existing ground.
fl.surface.missing: Off the surface, kept as they were: vertices {list}.
fl.even.done: The vertices between the first and the last now lie on one grade.
fl.undo.surface: Feature line elevations from the ground
pp.vex.lowered: The profile is drawn {used}× exaggerated, not {want}×, so its elevations fit on every sheet.
pp.vex.clipped: Even at 1× some elevations do not fit the profile window: they are cut off.
pp.ui.title: Plan and profile sheets: {name}
pp.ui.lede: Each sheet shows a stretch of the alignment twice: the plan above, turned so the road runs across the sheet, and the profile below at the same horizontal scale. Match lines join the sheets. One PDF, a page per sheet.

pp.ui.info.one: 1 sheet, up to {len} {u} of the alignment.

pp.ui.bad.range: Type a start and an end station, the end after the start.

pp.ui.done.one: Saved 1 plan and profile sheet as {file}.
pp.ui.done.other: Saved {n} plan and profile sheets as {file}.

pp.ui.no.alignment: The alignment has errors: fix it before making sheets.
codes.title: Description keys and line codes
codes.keys.lede: A key matches the field code at the start of a description (* = any characters, ? = one) and puts the point in a group, with a use and a long description. The first key that matches wins; codes no key matches stay their own group.
codes.col.label: Description
codes.lines.on: Join points into lines by line codes
codes.lines.lede: A line code is the word right after the field code: "EP B" begins a new edge-of-pavement line, "EP E" ends it, "BLDG C" closes a building back to its first corner. Points with the same code join in point-number order; EP1 and EP2 are separate lines. Breakline groups follow these lines; other groups' lines are drawn on the plan.

codes.done.one: 1 description key applied; the groups and the surface follow (Ctrl+Z undoes it).
codes.done.other: {keys} description keys applied; the groups and the surface follow (Ctrl+Z undoes it).

codes.dropped.one: 1 key with a code CivilCraft cannot read was left out (codes are letters, digits and * ? _ . - / #).
codes.dropped.other: {n} keys with codes CivilCraft cannot read were left out (codes are letters, digits and * ? _ . - / #).

v3d.map.noload: The map tools could not be loaded. Check the connection and try again.
s3.labels.cut: Only the first {n} labels are shown.
v3d.gis.cut: GIS layers have more than {n} line pieces: the rest is not drawn in 3D.

v3d.gis.off.other: {n} GIS shapes without elevations lie off the surface and are not drawn in 3D.

v3d.hint: 3D: drag to orbit, Shift+drag or right-drag to pan, the wheel zooms; click an alignment, pad, feature line, breakline, pipe, structure or point to select it.

kml.zip.empty: {file} holds no shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage or KML.
kml.empty: {file} has no placemarks with a geometry.
gis.label.on: {layer} is labeled with {field} (on the plan, in the PDF, DXF and DWG). Ctrl+Z undoes it.
map.out.pdf: Map layers under the plan (as a picture)
map.out.dwg: Map layers as a picture beside the drawing (downloads a .zip: the DWG, a PNG and its world file)
map.out.partial: Some map pictures had not arrived after 8 seconds: the map is incomplete; try again.
map.out.pdf.done: The map layers are under the linework.
map.out.dwg.done: The map layers are in {png} beside the drawing; the DWG shows it as an image on layer G-MAP-IMAG (keep the two files together).
grid.replaced: The previous surface was replaced; Ctrl+Z brings it back.
grid.replace.ask: The project's surface becomes the grid from {name}. Survey points stay as they are. You can undo it (Ctrl+Z).
tin.rebuild.undo: Rebuild the surface from the points
tin.rebuild.done: The surface is now built from the points. Ctrl+Z brings the file's surface back.
xs.none: No section to put on sheets: add sample lines to the alignment first.
xs.wide: The sections are wider than the paper at this scale: they are cut off at the sheet's edge. Choose a smaller scale or larger paper.
xs.vex: The sections are drawn {used}× exaggerated, not {want}×, so the tallest one fits on the sheet.
xs.strip: {name}: cross sections, sta {a} to {b}. Horizontal {h}, vertical {v} ({vex}× exaggerated)
xs.ui.title: Cross-section sheets: {name}
xs.ui.lede: Every section of the alignment on PDF pages, in rows: the ground, the design, cut and fill shaded, the corridor points, each section's station and areas under it.

xs.ui.done.one: Saved 1 page of cross sections as {file}.
xs.ui.done.other: Saved {n} pages of cross sections as {file}.

se.short: Curve {n} (radius {r}) is too short for full superelevation: the transitions meet before it is reached.
se.overlap: The superelevation transitions of curves {a} and {b} overlap: lengthen the tangent between them, or check the rate table.
se.head: Superelevation
se.off.note: With superelevation on, the lanes rotate about the centerline through each curve: the outside lane flattens, then the whole road tilts toward the inside of the curve, and back after it.
se.rate.e.of: Superelevation rate of row {n}, in percent (empty = normal crown)
se.rate.note: A curve takes the rate of the first row whose radius it reaches. These rates and the 0.5 % gradient are placeholders, not a standard: set them from your own design criteria. Runoff = lane width × e ÷ the gradient; runout = normal crown ÷ e × runoff; two thirds of the runoff lies before the curve.
se.none: No curve of this alignment is sharp enough to superelevate with this table.
se.diagram.label: Superelevation diagram: the left lane's cross slope (solid) and the right lane's (dashed) along the stations; down = falls away from the center line.
co.note: Both sides alike, slopes falling away from the crown. Placeholders, not a standard. Superelevation is below; curb and gutter, sidewalks and widening are not available yet.
hy.no.outlet: {name} drains to no structure of the network: choose its outlet.
hy.loop: The pipes form a loop, so flows cannot be summed downstream: break the loop.
hy.full: {name} flows full (surcharged): the hydraulic grade line is above its crown.
hy.flood: The hydraulic grade line is {by} above the rim at {name}: water reaches the surface there.
dr.head: Storm drainage
dr.note: Q = C × i × A, summed down the network: each pipe carries every catchment above it at the longest time of concentration, with travel times through the pipes flowing full. i in {i}, Q in {q}, A in {a}. The intensity curve, n and the junction loss are placeholders, not a standard: set them from your own rainfall data and design criteria.
dr.hint: Catchment: click the corners of the area that drains to a structure. Enter finishes; it drains to a structure inside it, else the nearest one.
dr.none: No catchments yet. Draw the areas that drain to each structure to work out flows, pipe sizes and the hydraulic grade line.
dr.c.head: Catchment
dr.c.name: Name
dr.c.note: C is the share of the rain that runs off (0 to 1). The time of concentration is how long water takes from the farthest point of the area to its structure.
dr.c.few: A catchment needs at least three corners.
dr.c.nonet: Draw the pipe network first: a catchment drains to one of its structures.
dr.c.drawn: {name}: {a}, draining to {to}, C 0.5. Change them in Properties.
dr.ok: Every pipe flows part full and the hydraulic grade line stays below every rim.
dr.size: Size the pipes for these flows
dr.size.note: Each pipe gets the smallest standard size that carries its flow at its own slope. Inverts stay where they are: set them again from the rules if the sizes change.
dr.size.same: Every pipe already has the smallest size that carries its flow.
dr.size.done: {n} pipe sizes changed (one step: Ctrl+Z undoes it).
dr.size.bad: {n} pipes need more than the largest size: make them steeper or split the flow.
dr.idf.lead: Rainfall intensity for the design storm, as i = a ÷ (tc + b) to the power c:
dr.idf.formula: Fit a, b and c to your own intensity-duration-frequency curve for the return period you design for.
pc.err.radius: A curve needs its radius: R 300.
pc.err.turn: Say which way the curve turns: left or right.
pc.err.delta: A curve needs its arc length (L 52.36) or its central angle (D 10°00'00").
pc.err.bearing: This bearing cannot be read: write it as N 45°30'15" E, or AZ 45°30'15".
pc.err.dist: The distance must be more than zero.
pc.err.read: This line cannot be read: write a bearing and a distance (N 45°30'15" E 125.50), or a curve (C R 300 L 52.36 right).
pc.pob.at: a point at northing {n}, easting {e}, the point of beginning
pc.call.left: along a curve to the left, having a radius of {r}, an arc length of {l}, a central angle of {delta}, and a chord bearing and distance of {cb}, {cd}
pc.call.right: along a curve to the right, having a radius of {r}, an arc length of {l}, a central angle of {delta}, and a chord bearing and distance of {cb}, {cd}
pc.head: Parcels
pc.none: No parcels yet. Draw one by its corners, or enter the calls from a deed or plat.
pc.name: Name
pc.c.radius.of: Radius of course {n} (empty = a straight line)
pc.c.note: Type a radius to make a course a curve through the same two corners (empty makes it straight again). A curve to the right has its center to the right of the direction of travel, as in a deed. Courses run from the point of beginning, the first corner, round the parcel.
pc.legal.note: A draft from the drawing, not a survey: a licensed surveyor has to check it against the record and sign it before it is used.
pc.copy.select: Copying is blocked here: the text is selected, press Ctrl+C.
pc.few: A parcel needs at least three corners.
pc.drawn: {name}: {area}. Its courses and legal description are in Properties.
pc.dlg.title: Parcel from deed calls
pc.dlg.or: or at a northing and easting:
pc.dlg.help: One call a line: a bearing and a distance (N 45°30'15" E 125.50), or a curve (C R 300 L 52.36 right, or with D 10°00'00" for its central angle; add CB and a bearing when it is not tangent to the course before it). "thence", commas and "feet" are fine; # starts a comment.
pc.dlg.nostart: Say where the calls start: a survey point, or a northing and easting.
pc.dlg.badne: The northing and easting must be numbers.
pc.dlg.gap: The calls do not come back to where they started: the parcel closes with a straight course across the gap. Check the calls against the deed.
pc.dlg.done.gap: {name} from the calls: {area}. They do not close: the last course crosses the gap.
pc.hint: Parcel: click its corners, starting at the point of beginning (a click near a survey point takes its place). Enter finishes.
pc.props.head: Parcel
pc.click.point: Corner {k} at survey point {n}. Click the next corner; Enter (or the first corner again) finishes.
pc.click: Corner {k}. Click the next corner; Enter (or the first corner again) finishes.
tv.err.closebearing: A closing angle only checks angles: with bearings there is nothing to close.
tv.err.angle: This angle cannot be read: write it as 270°00'10", 270-00-10, 270 00 10 or 270.0028 (under 360°).
tv.err.read: This line cannot be read: write the bearing, then the distance (N 45°30'15" E 125.50).
tv.err.bearing: This bearing cannot be read: write it as N 45°30'15" E, or AZ 45-30-15.
tv.err.dist: A leg needs a distance more than zero after its angle.
tv.few: A traverse needs at least two legs.
tv.head: Traverse
tv.lede: Enter field angles or bearings and distances: CivilCraft checks the closure, adjusts by the compass rule and adds the stations as survey points or a parcel.
tv.title: Traverse
tv.ends.pt.num: Number of the survey point it ends on
tv.help.angles: One leg a line: the angle right turned at the station the leg leaves (clockwise from the station behind to the next one), the distance, and a name for the station it reaches if you like: 270°00'10" 125.50 B. Angles as 270-00-10, 270 00 10 or 270.0028 work too. On a loop, end with "close" and the angle at the start again (from the last station to the second) to check the angles.
tv.help.bearings: One leg a line: the bearing, the distance, and a name for the station it reaches if you like: N 45°30'15" E 125.50 B. Azimuths as one word work too: AZ 45-30-15.
tv.err.bs: Say where the angles start from: a backsight survey point, or its azimuth.
tv.err.bsaz: The backsight azimuth cannot be read: write it as 90°00'00" or 90-00-00 (under 360°).
tv.err.end: Say which survey point the traverse ends on.
tv.noclose: not checked: add a closing angle (close 270°00'05")
tv.more: {n} more stations are in the report.
tv.compass: Coordinates after the compass rule: the angular misclosure is spread equally over the angles, then the linear misclosure over the legs in proportion to their lengths.
tv.added: {n} traverse stations added as survey points {first} to {last} (description TRAV, no elevation). Ctrl+Z takes them out.
sk.strip: {name}   {n} stakes   offsets L = left, R = right of the alignment; C = cut, F = fill ({u})
sk.title: staking report
sk.noal: Finish the alignment first: it needs at least two points.
sk.src.grid: stations and offsets along the alignment
sk.keys: Also at the alignment's key stations (where curves begin and end)
sk.pts.note: Every survey point within this distance of the alignment, with its station and offset, the design there and its own elevation as the ground: an as-staked or as-built check.
sk.design.corr: Design elevations come from the graded corridor, from daylight line to daylight line, else the design profile on the centerline; ground elevations from the existing surface (a survey point's own elevation when staking points). Cut = ground above design.
sk.design.prof: Design elevations come from the design profile on the centerline (this alignment has no corridor, so offsets have none); ground elevations from the existing surface (a survey point's own elevation when staking points). Cut = ground above design.
sk.err.sta: The stations cannot be read: write them as 1+50 or 150.
sk.err.step: The interval must be more than zero.
sk.err.off: This offset cannot be read: {tok}. Write offsets as 12 L, 0, 12 R (or -12, 0, 12).
sk.err.nooff: Give at least one offset (0 is the centerline).
sk.err.first: The first number must be a whole number.
sk.err.many: {n} stakes is too many for one report: use a longer interval or a shorter range.
sk.err.near: The distance must be more than zero.
sk.err.nopts: No survey points are that close to the alignment.
sk.nodesign: {n} stakes have no design elevation there, so no cut or fill.
sk.saved.csv: Staking report saved as CSV: {n} stakes.
sk.saved.pdf: Staking report saved as PDF: {n} stakes on {p} pages.
sk.more: {n} more stakes are in the report.
dv.title: Drive along an alignment: the view from a driver's seat on the road
dv.none: There is no alignment to drive: draw one first (Alignment, A).
dv.on.prof: Driving {name} on its design profile. Space plays or pauses, ← and → step, Esc stops.
dv.on.eg: Driving {name} on the existing ground: it has no design profile yet. Space plays or pauses, ← and → step, Esc stops.
dv.off: Back to the view you had.
sun.title: Light the site from where the sun is at a date and time
sun.need: Type the site's latitude and longitude (degrees; south and west are minus).
sun.need.crs: Type the site's latitude and longitude (degrees; south and west are minus), or set the project's coordinate system to have them filled in.
sun.at: Sun at azimuth {az}°, {alt}° above the horizon.
sun.below: The sun is below the horizon (azimuth {az}°).
sun.fromcrs: Latitude and longitude from the project's coordinate system.
sun.note: Clock time in the time zone you pick; daylight saving is up to you. Positions from NOAA's solar equations.
grid.shift.on: From the grid shift file {name}: NAD27 to NAD83 within about {acc} inside the grid (outside it, no shift), and NAD83 is taken as WGS 84 (about a meter or two).
grid.shift.missing: The grid shift file {name} is named but not loaded here: the rough shift is used until it is added again below.
grid.head: Grid shift file
grid.none: None: the shift from this datum to WGS 84 is a rough one (for NAD27 about 20 m). A grid shift file makes latitude and longitude, GIS files and map layers land within about 10 cm of NAD83.
grid.using: Using {name} ({kind}), covering longitude {w} to {e}, latitude {s} to {n}.
grid.inside: The project's middle is inside the grid.
grid.outside: The project's middle is outside this grid: there, no shift is applied at all. Use a grid that covers the site.
grid.note: NTv2 (.gsb) and PROJ GeoTIFF grids (.tif, as cdn.proj.org serves them) are read. The grid is saved in the project file. Downloading sends only the grid's file name to cdn.proj.org. GIS layers already imported stay where they are; import them again to place them with the grid.
grid.done: {name} is the project's datum shift now: one step, Ctrl+Z undoes it.
grid.offdone: The grid is no longer used: the rough shift is back. Ctrl+Z undoes it.
grid.fetch.fail: The grid could not be downloaded ({msg}). Download it yourself and use Add a grid file.
grid.big: That file is over 20 MB: CivilCraft keeps grids up to 20 MB in a project. Use a grid for the site's region.
grid.s.conus: NADCON5, NAD27 to NAD83, conterminous United States
grid.err.name: A grid needs a file name.
grid.err.kind: This is not a grid shift file: CivilCraft reads NTv2 (.gsb) and PROJ GeoTIFF grids (.tif).
grid.err.empty: The grid file has no grids in it.
grid.err.notinfile: The grid shift file {name} is not in the project file: add it again under GIS › Coordinates (until then the rough shift is used).
grid.err.badfile: The grid shift file in the project file could not be read.
mh.title: Mass haul: {name}
mh.factor: Shrink (−) or swell (+) of the cut
mh.factor.note: What a cubic yard of cut makes once placed and compacted as fill: −10 % means it shrinks to 0.9. It is a placeholder, not a standard: use your geotechnical report's figure. Volumes are the sample lines' (average end areas).
mh.diagram.label: Mass-haul diagram: the running total of cut (after shrink or swell) less fill along the stations; above zero, earth to move up station; below, down station.
mh.totals: Cut {cut} ({adj} after shrink or swell), fill {fill}.
mh.waste: {v} of cut is left over: waste.
mh.nobalance: No balance point: the earth never balances between the ends.
mh.nospans: Nothing to move: no cut and no fill along the sample lines.

touch.back.done.=0: Took the last point back; none left.
touch.back.done.one: Took the last point back; {n} point left.
touch.back.done.other: Took the last point back; {n} points left.

san.p.flat: {name} has no fall: set its inverts (Set every invert from the rules).
san.p.over: {name} is {pct}% full at the peak flow; the limit is {max}%.
san.p.slow: {name} runs at {v} at the peak flow, slower than the {min} minimum (it may not clean itself).
san.p.fast: {name} runs at {v} at the peak flow, faster than the {max} maximum.
san.lead: Peak flows for a sanitary sewer: the people and area entering at each structure, summed downstream, times a flow per person and a peaking factor, plus infiltration. Steady peak flow only; no routing over time.
san.note: P is the population in thousands. These starting values are placeholders, not a standard: set your agency's. Velocities are at the peak flow's own depth (Manning, constant n).
san.none: No flows yet: select a structure and enter the people and area that enter there.
san.size.note: Size the pipes for these flows picks, for each pipe, the smallest standard size whose full capacity times the limit above carries its peak flow, at the pipe's own slope.
san.s.note: For shops, offices or industry, enter equivalent people (area × people per area your agency uses). The area counts for infiltration.
san.head: Sanitary design flows
san.ok: Every pipe carries its peak flow within the limits.
